result.summary: Pausanias walks through Sparta, listing hero-chapels, tombs and temples. He recounts Hercules' quarrel with Hippocoon and his sons, and describes odd statues of Enyalius in fetters and Aphrodite in fetters.

scenes.title: Hero-chapels near Platanistas
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the chapels of Cynisca and the sons of Hippocoon, the tomb of Alcman, and the temples of Helen and Hercules.

scenes.title: Hercules against Hippocoon
scenes.summary: Hercules' feud with Hippocoon's sons arises from their refusal to cleanse him and from the killing of Œonus. After his vengeance he builds a temple to Athene.
scenes.stakes: Œonus is killed; Hercules risks defeat and wounds in his fight with Hippocoon's sons.

scenes.title: Temples of Athene, Enyalius, Hera
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Theras' temple, Hipposthenes' shrine, the fettered Enyalius, the Painted Lounge chapels, and Hera Goateater.

scenes.title: Aphrodite in fetters
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes temples near the theatre and the armed, fettered Aphrodite, rejecting the story that Tyndareus punished her.

alias_notes.explanation: Cult title of Athene at Sparta, given after Hercules' vengeance.
Spartan cult title of Hera, linked to goat sacrifices.
Title of Aphrodite in her upper-story shrine.

notable_quotes.reason: Explains the Spartan and Athenian logic of binding or wingless statues to keep war or victory.
Pausanias rationally dismisses the story of punishing a goddess through her statue.

analysis.text: The passage links Spartan monuments to heroic myth, showing how cult sites preserved memory of Hercules' feud and local lineages.
The fettered statues reflect a belief that binding an image could keep a deity's favour in the city.

fun_facts.text: Cynisca's Olympic victories were won by horses she owned, since women could not compete in person.

language_notes.text: A hero-chapel (heroon) was a shrine honouring a dead person as a hero, who received cult offerings.
The Lacedæmonian dialect is the Doric Greek of Sparta, which Pausanias calls harsh-sounding; Alcman nonetheless wrote his choral songs in it.
"Clear himself" means to be ritually purified of blood-guilt after a killing, which Greek custom required.
"Exactor of due punishment" translates a cult title of Athene, meaning she who exacts penalty or requital.
Thera is the modern Santorini; Theras led Spartan settlers there, which explains the Spartan cult of Athene linked to him and the old name Calliste ('fairest').
Hipposthenes is honoured like Poseidon on an oracle's command; the comparison suggests he receives divine-style sacrifice, though he was a mortal athlete.
Wingless Victory refers to the statue of Nike at Athens, kept wingless so victory could not fly away.
A 'Lounge' (Greek lesche) was a public meeting hall where men gathered to talk; 'hero-chapel' means a shrine to a heroized dead person.
'Goateater' is a cult title of Hera; the epithet pairs with the unusual sacrifice of goats, which the following sentences explain.
'Tutelary' means guardian or protecting; here it is Poseidon's cult title at Sparta.
'The Shapely' translates Aphrodite's cult epithet Morpho, a title also tied to beauty of form.

context_notes.text: Cynisca won the four-horse chariot race at Olympia in the early fourth century BC. Owners, not drivers, were named victors, so women could win.
Alcman was a Spartan lyric poet of the seventh century BC, famous for choral songs for maidens.
Alcmena was Hercules' mother. Œonus was the son of her brother Licymnius.
Tisamenus, son of Orestes, was a Spartan ruler in the legend of the Heraclidae's return; Amphilochus was a seer and hero of the Trojan and Theban saga.
Hercules fought Hippocoon and his sons at Sparta after they killed his kinsman; Hera was famously hostile to Hercules throughout his life.
Tyndareus was king of Sparta and the legal father of Helen and Clytemnestra, whose scandals the rival story blames on Aphrodite.

literary_notes.text: Sweetness of poetry is set against the harshness of the dialect, praising Alcman's skill by contrast.
The vivid small incident of a dog and a stone shows how a trivial act sparks a deadly feud.
The fettered god and the wingless goddess symbolise a city's wish to bind victory to itself; the chains and missing wings stand for permanence.
The 'bonds of love' turns the statue's fetters into an image of love's power to bind men to women.
Pausanias mocks the punishment story: striking a small cedar image would hardly punish a goddess, and his sarcastic tone makes the idea look foolish.
